utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now in hearing. Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. Please, Madam Registrar, can you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-17-A, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Bralo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Bralo, can you hear and follow the proceedings in a language that you understand? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can sit down. I would like now to have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Xavier Tracol, together with Mr. Peter Kremer, QC, senior substitute, and Lourdes Galicia, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me turn to the Defence for Mr. Bralo. Can you please introduce yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Jonathan Cooper, lead counsel for Mr. Bralo, and I'm assisted by Virginia Lindsay, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In this case, Mr. Bralo appealed the sentencing judgement against him on -- issued on 7th of December, 2005. He is now awaiting the Appeals decision and is detained in the UN Detention Unit here in The Hague in the Netherlands. Further to Rule 65 bis (B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, an Appeals Status Conference is convened in the 120 days following the filing of the appeals notice so that the detained person awaiting their -- the appeals decision may raise any questions related to the appeal. The order convening the present Status Conference was issued on the 2nd of May, 2006. So this is the first time that we are meeting today, and I wish to ask Mr. Bralo, if he so wishes, whether he has any concerns in relation to the detention conditions or his state of health. Mr. Bralo, please, do you wish to take the floor? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] I have nothing I would like to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Bralo. Let us now look into the progress in this appeals proceeding. You know that we are waiting for a notice or -- by the appeal to reply to the respondent's brief, which was filed on the 2nd of May, 2006. On Friday, we received the appellant's application for leave to file his brief in reply within the 15 days as of the date the documents were disclosed further to the Appeals Chamber decision on the appellant's motion for leave to access to the certified file in the first instance. Excuse me. It was the motion to gain access to the said -- to the Trial Chamber's documents. I note that under Rule 113, this filing, the filing of your brief, should be done by the 12th of May. That is, within the 10 days from the date the brief -- the respondent's brief was filed. I also note that the appeals status -- or Pre-Appeals Judge can change any time limit decided on for the filing of submissions if good cause is shown. The appellant argues that it would be justified to have the time limit postponed because the Defence are still waiting for documents to be disclosed further to the Appeals Chamber's decision of 2nd of May, and also that the first Defence counsel was not able to use the days that he had in order to prepare for the brief in reply because he had to come to The Hague for this Status Conference. That's right, isn't it? To save time, I would rather rule on this application orally. However, prior to doing so, I would ask the Prosecutor to express his view on this application.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution opposes this motion by the Defence because they're asking for two postponements. First, they are requiring 15 days, and not 10 days as the Rules would demand, and the starting point would be as of the time when the documents are disclosed and not as of the time when the Prosecution filed their brief in reply. In our view, good cause was not shown as under the Rule to obtain such a postponement. The first ground is indeed that the appellant's counsel had to come to The Hague for this Status Conference, but it was very easy for counsel -- for Defence counsel to work whilst they were travelling on the draft of their brief in reply. The second ground that is argued prompts me to say this: The scope of the brief in reply is the brief filed by the Prosecution and not the documents. You said that documents were to be disclosed to the Defence, but if the Defence were to argue with further arguments based on the said documents which are to be disclosed, of course the Prosecution would like to be in a position to meet those arguments. If such arguments are filed within the brief in reply, we will not be able to present such a response. You ordered disclosure to be effected, but in a redacted way. The Prosecution, last Friday, filed these documents with the Registry in electronic form. They are, therefore, to be transmitted to the Defence further to the decision by the Appeals Chamber, and this will be done by the Registry. There are altogether 187 pages, but -- there are -- [B/C/S on English channel] among those that we have to give to the Defence, and you have them in various languages; in French, in English, and also in B/C/S. Therefore, as to the actual amount of documents to be taken under scrutiny by the Defence is not 187 but 100 pages, around 100 pages. So there's no justification for an extension of the time limit as requested by the Defence, which is 15 days as of the date of disclosure. So this is our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tracol. Let me turn to the Defence. Do you have any submissions following the statements by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do, and I'm grateful for the opportunity. Firstly, the judgement that Your Honour kindly made in her decision in relation to disclosure made quite clear that disclosure should be made in the interests of justice of a number of documents, whether it's a hundred pages or a hundred and fifty pages. These are documents which are of importance for disclosure to the appellant, and plainly they are only of use to the appellant if the appellant is in a position to make use of them and to make use of them in the simplest and most elegant way. It's clear that the Prosecution envisages reference to these documents in the reply brief, and if there is material newly disclosed, then that seems to be the most appropriate mechanism for getting that material to the Court. Of course, if it's necessary to enable the Prosecution to be able to make further representations about anything new which emerges in the course of the reply brief, then it's plainly appropriate that the Prosecution should be able to do so. But as is quite clear from Your Honour's judgement, this material is not only appropriate for disclosure now, but it should have been disclosed at a much earlier stage in these proceedings. And of course, had it been so disclosed, then there'd be no question of it being referred to at this late stage. So the Defence have to catch up with this material. Despite Your Honour's ruling, there has as yet been no disclosure. The material needs to be look at, it needs to be considered, and it needs to be presented, if necessary, to the Court in the most appropriate form. So it's my submission that the normal length of time for reply, which is normally 10 days, should be extended by a small amount to 15 days and that the date on which that time period should run should start from compliance with Your Honour's ruling, because otherwise one might be in a position where a reply is filed and then, as a result of late honouring of -- of the direction that Your Honour has given, that there would be a need for a further exchange of filings, and in my submission that would be unfortunate. As to the secondary basis, plainly it's very helpful indeed to have an opportunity to attend the Trial Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber, to be able to have productive meetings between Defence and Prosecution, and to be able to raise matters with the Pre-Appeal Judge. It's an opportunity which we value. Unfortunately, falling in the middle of the 10-day period causes practical difficulties, and I can assure counsel for the Prosecution that it's wholly impossible to conduct effective work in the course of transit either to the airport, in the aeroplane from London to Amsterdam, or on the train, and that is wholly unrealistic. And the practical position is that the Defence team loses three days out of 10. We are doing good business whilst I'm present in The Hague, but, unfortunately, substantive progress on the reply is affected. So it's for those reasons that I submit that it is appropriate to extend time. In my submission, it's helpful giving the parties, within reason, the time that's necessary in order to give the best possible assistance to the Appeals Chamber. So unless I can assist Your Honour further on that, those are the submissions that I make in relation to that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You were very clear indeed. I would, nevertheless ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was saying that I'd like to ask Madam Registrar, who apparently has received the documents from the Prosecutor, I'd like to ask her when this can be disclosed to the Defence. Is it possible to have an answer right now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The documents will be handed over to the Defence later this afternoon, some of the documents, and the rest will be available from the judicial database hopefully by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. We note that the Prosecution does not want the time period to be extended. However, on the basis of the submissions by the Defence, who is still awaiting for the documents to be disclosed whilst they were supposed to receive such documents further to our decision of the 2nd of May, we feel that it is necessary for the time period to be extended by 10 days, running as of the day when the documents are disclosed. So you can do the calculations yourselves. By way of a reminder, the issue of the length of the brief is that you have to have at most 3.000 words. And do not forget that a brief in reply only contains submissions responding to the arguments put in the respondent's brief and, therefore, should not present any new arguments, any new points of fact or law. As regards the appellant's brief which was filed confidentially on the 30th of March, 2006, further to paragraph 1 of the Practice Direction on the length of briefs and motions, an appellant's brief, when appealing a sentencing judgement, should not be longer than 12.000 words. I note that the appellant's brief is longer than the said amount by 3.000 words. I am the Pre-Appeals Judge. I can authorise an additional amount but only in the presence of exceptional circumstances that would justify longer filings. Can you give us any explanations in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, and I'm grateful for the opportunity to -- to do so. I hope the expression "mea culpa" translates into every language which is being translated around the courtroom today, and it's simply this: The Practice Direction of the 16th of September was simply not noted by myself. Of course it should have been and the word count should have been adhered to. The applicable word count is, of course, 12.000 words, and Your Honour will note that the appeal brief as filed contains some rather extensive quotation within the body of the appeal brief from documents which are in fact appended to the appeal brief as a series of appendices, and if Your Honour was so minded to order us to comply with the word limit, then we would be able to do so and we would simply excise a number of the quotes, make reference to the appendices; and as I indicated, we will of course comply with Your Honour's direction to us in any respect. That said, I wonder if it's necessary to direct us to do that. The appeal brief reads as it does because that was considered by myself and my co-counsel to be the best way of advancing the arguments, and it may simply make it a little more difficult for appeal Judges to consider those arguments if some of the quotations are excised and taken to a different part of the brief. Nothing I say should be taken as other than a completely full apology, and I think there's nothing I should add or can add to my submissions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Cooper. What is your position, Mr. Tracol? Do you think that this extension should be authorised?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has answered this in the brief in reply of the 2nd of May. Particularly footnote number 17 does address this matter. The Prosecution does not oppose an excessive number of words, but we have noted that the Defence counsel has not followed the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tracol. Mr. Cooper, can you tell us whether you need any more time if you have to file a shorter reply brief? If you are to file a shorter reply brief, do you need more time? I can repeat the question if you like. If you need to file a new brief, a shorter brief, do you need more time to file this reply brief or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I think, since it's my mistake, I will be as swift as I possibly can in correcting that mistake if Your Honour deems it necessary and so, no, that would not affect the time limit for the reply. I would, I suppose, simply ask for perhaps seven days to file a corrected appeal brief within the relevant time limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In light of the position expressed by both parties, even though the submissions that substantiate the additional amount of time are not exceptional circumstances pursuant to the directive, I have noted that in the interests of judicial economy and in the interest of the progress of this case, I consider the appellant's brief filed in a valid manner. We would also like to ask the Defence whether it has any intention to file a public appellant's brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, we do. And indeed, a draft version of the public version is already available, and we anticipate being in a position to do that within the next few days. The reason that we've held off from doing that until now is because there is a corrigendum, a correction, to the appeal brief which should be filed first, and it includes two very minor matters, but they're matters that should be corrected before the -- before the appeal brief is put into its public version. Again, simply to save the economy of the page count. And if I can assist Your Honour with those, briefly it's simply this: There is a mistyping in my paragraph 77 of the appeal brief. I won't take Your Honour to it now, but it's simply the addition of a rogue word that should not have been in that paragraph. Separately, in Appendix G, and again I don't take Your Honour to that now, of three pages that should have been filed, only one of them was included in the filed copy. So there need to be an addition of two pages probably as a page whatever it is, 230 bis and 230 ter so they can fit in with the current pagination of the appeal brief. So I was intending to raise that matter again. I hoped to be able to raise that with my learned friends with the Prosecution to see whether it was necessary to file a formal corrigendum of the entire appeal brief or whether I should file simply the pages which need to be corrected. So again, my apologies for the fact that this clearing-up operation has to be done, but I think these are not central issues. And again, I hope to be able to deal with those in the simplest way and in accordance with Your Honour's direction and any latitude that the Prosecution may feel it appropriate to suggest. So the answer to Your Honour's question, public brief available to be filed certainly in the next few days. I would like it to be a public brief which is a final version. So if it becomes necessary to take longer over the correction, then of course I'll do that and file the public brief immediately afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Cooper. Prosecutor, I don't know if you wish to say something on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The Appendix G which has been introduced in the appellant's brief are excerpts of the transcript of General Blaskic's testimony in his own trial. These transcript excerpts are not presented in a legal manner because they're not part and parcel of the documents that have been tendered into evidence and when the sentence was rendered by the Trial Chamber. If the Defence wishes these documents to be adduced to the Appeals Chamber, the Defence may then file a motion pursuant to Rule 115 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence to which the Prosecution will provide a response in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Prosecutor. I think that Mr. Cooper has listened to you. You have been very precise, namely when you mention Appendix G. So if you would like to file a motion before the Chamber, we should then look into the motion in question. As far as the corrigendum is concerned, we feel that you may correct points when these are not of any substance. This corrigendum procedure may enable you to correct some typing errors. This, nonetheless, does not affect the substance of the document. I would now like to ask the parties whether they have any questions -- any other questions. I think I have, broadly speaking, addressed all the items I wanted to address with you today. Prosecutor, do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no questions, Your Honour. Just I'd like to clarify something. In light of the decision you rendered today, you granted 10 days to the Defence starting on the date at which the documents would be disclosed. The registrar representative told us that those documents that have been corrected were presented today, but I -- those redacted documents provided by the Registry will be provided tomorrow. So from when -- what date or when does this extension run from, from today or from tomorrow? Is it when the redacted documents are being presented or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must reckon that it is once all the documents have been disclosed. Undoubtedly tomorrow, given what Madam Registrar has just told us. Do you have any other questions? No further questions. Mr. Cooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Simply this: As to the question of disclosure, I'm going to address, if I may, some other disclosure requests that will be made, and I simply raise this at this time to put the Court on notice that there will be further disclosure requests made by the appellant in the normal way, supported by filings. These without -- if I were to go into the details, that would require us to go into a closed session, and it is not necessary to do that at this stage. But Your Honour will appreciate that there were a number of questions which were raised in the course of the appeal brief in relation to, for example, the use that was made of a number of documents that were handed over by Mr. Bralo in 1997, and the Prosecution have replied in the -- responded in the particular way that they did in their response. That response does not, in our view, adequately answer the question raised in the appeal brief, and we feel that the appropriate course, then, is to make a further application for additional disclosure in respect of three distinct areas, and so Your Honour may expect a filing dealing with that matter within a short time. Please rest assured that the appellant and Prosecution have discussed the nature of the obligation to disclose and there appear to be some significant differences between the appellant's and the Prosecutor's position in relation to this. That's the only other matter that appears to be outstanding at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cooper. If it is necessary, you may file motions with the Chamber, and the Chamber will then respond to these motions. For the time being, we are asking the parties to try and get closer and to try and sort out these disclosure issues. If there are no further questions, we shall adjourn this Status Conference, and we would like to thank all the parties, as well as all those people who have given us a helping hand today. The court stands adjourned.
